title: Children of Abraham by Faith
summary: Paul appeals to the Galatians' own experience: they received the Spirit by believing the message about the crucified Christ, not by keeping the law. He then argues from Scripture that Abraham was counted righteous by faith, that the law brings a curse Christ bore on the cross, and that the law, given 430 years after the promise, cannot cancel it. The law served as a temporary guardian until Christ; now all who belong to Christ by faith are sons of God, one in him, and heirs of Abraham's promise.
story: Having finished his personal story in chapters 1 and 2, Paul now turns to argument, and the argument reaches all the way back to Genesis. The teachers troubling the Galatians evidently claimed that to be true children of Abraham, Gentile believers must be circumcised, as Abraham was, and keep the law given through Moses. Paul answers by retelling Israel's story in order: first the promise to Abraham, received by faith; then, centuries later, the law at Sinai; then the coming of Christ, the promised seed, who bore the law's curse and opened the blessing to the nations. The chapter is one of the Bible's great summaries of how the Old Testament story leads to Christ, and it prepares for chapter 4, where Paul presses the same point through the pictures of heirs, sons, and slaves.
historical:
The Galatian believers were Gentiles who had turned from the gods of their cities to the God of Israel through Paul's preaching. Whether they lived in the old ethnic region of Galatia in central Asia Minor (the North Galatian view) or in the southern cities of the Roman province of Galatia that Paul visited in Acts 13 and 14, such as Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe (the South Galatian view), is debated. Either way, they had experienced dramatic evidence of God's presence, including miracles (v. 5), and had apparently suffered for their faith (v. 4).

The number 430 years (v. 17) comes from Exodus 12:40, which gives the length of Israel's stay in Egypt. Paul uses it simply to show that the law came long after the promise; he is not making a point about the exact chronology. The idea that the law was delivered through angels (v. 19) also appears in Stephen's speech in Acts 7:53 and in Hebrews 2:2, and reflects a Jewish tradition drawn from texts such as Deuteronomy 33:2.
cultural:
Paul's language draws on everyday life. Bewitched (v. 1) translates a word associated with the evil eye, a widespread ancient belief that a malicious look could cast a spell; Paul uses it ironically to ask who has put them under such a spell. Clearly portrayed (v. 1) uses a verb that could describe a public notice posted for everyone to see: Paul's preaching had set the crucified Christ before them as plainly as a placard.

A human covenant or will (v. 15), once ratified, could not be altered by a later party. The guardian of verses 24 and 25 (paidagogos) was a household slave in Greek and Roman families who supervised a boy's behavior, escorted him to school, and disciplined him until he came of age. He was not the teacher and not the father; his role was temporary and protective, and a grown son no longer needed him. Paul's picture is that the law had such a role for Israel until Christ came. Hanging on a tree (v. 13) quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, where the body of an executed criminal exposed on a tree was declared cursed; by the first century the verse was connected with crucifixion.
literary: The chapter moves from rhetorical questions to scriptural argument. Verses 1 to 5 fire a series of questions that force the Galatians to admit they received the Spirit by faith. Verses 6 to 14 build a chain of Old Testament quotations: Genesis 15:6 and Genesis 12:3 (faith and blessing), Deuteronomy 27:26 (the curse on those who do not keep the law), Habakkuk 2:4 (the righteous live by faith), Leviticus 18:5 (the law is about doing), and Deuteronomy 21:23 (the curse on one hung on a tree). Verses 15 to 25 use a legal analogy and then answer an objection, “Why then was the law given?”, with a picture of the law's temporary role. The chapter closes in verses 26 to 29 with a confession of identity: sons of God, clothed with Christ, one in him, Abraham's seed. Paul's argument about the singular seed (v. 16) plays on a collective noun that can mean one descendant or many, a way of reading common in Jewish interpretation of his day.

outline.t: The Galatians received the Spirit by faith
Abraham believed God, and the nations are blessed
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law
The law cannot cancel the promise
Why the law was given: a guardian until Christ
One in Christ, heirs of the promise

doctrines.note: God's covenant promise to Abraham comes first and is not canceled by the later law of Moses. The promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham finds its fulfillment when Gentiles receive the Spirit by faith in Christ.
The law was holy and had a real purpose, but a limited one: it exposed transgression, held Israel in custody, and served as a guardian until Christ came. It was never able to give life (v. 21).

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (v. 13). This is one of the clearest statements in Paul of Christ's death as substitution: he took on himself the curse that belonged to others.
From Abraham onward, God counts people righteous through faith, trusting what God has promised. Faith is not a new invention of the church but the pattern of Abraham's own life.

words.note: Epangelia, promise. It appears eight times in this chapter. Paul contrasts promise with law: a promise depends on the one who makes it, while law depends on those who keep it. God's promise to Abraham, freely given, is the foundation of everything, and the Spirit himself is the promised gift (v. 14).

Sperma, seed or offspring. The word can mean one descendant or a whole line of descendants. Paul argues that the promise pointed finally to one seed, Christ (v. 16), and then that all who belong to Christ are, in him, Abraham's seed (v. 29). The one and the many meet in Christ.

Katara, curse. In the covenant of Deuteronomy, blessings followed obedience and curses followed disobedience. Paul says those who rely on works of the law stand under that curse, and that Christ took it on himself on the cross.

Paidagogos, guardian or custodian: the household slave who oversaw a child until he came of age. The older rendering schoolmaster can mislead, since the guardian was not primarily a teacher. The word pictures the law as protective and temporary.

christ: This chapter reads the whole Old Testament story as leading to Christ. He is the seed to whom the promise to Abraham referred (v. 16), the one through whom the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles (v. 14), and the one who redeemed his people from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for them on the cross (v. 13). In him the Spirit is given, and in him the divisions of the old order lose their power to rank people before God: all who are baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with him and are one in him (vv. 27-28). The link to Abraham is not a clever reading imposed afterward; Genesis itself promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, and Paul sees that promise kept in Jesus.

hard.q: Does “neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female” (3:28) erase all differences between people?
hard.a:
The verse is one of the most quoted in Paul, and readers draw different conclusions from it. In context Paul is talking about who belongs to God's family and on what basis: everyone who is in Christ by faith is a son of God and an heir, with no ranking according to ethnicity, social status, or sex. The three pairs echo divisions that structured ancient life, and some scholars note they may echo a Jewish prayer tradition that thanked God for not being made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman.

Paul elsewhere still addresses Jews and Gentiles, slaves and masters, husbands and wives as such, so most interpreters agree the verse does not mean these distinctions simply vanish. Christians disagree about what follows from it. Some, often called egalitarians, see the verse as a principle whose implications include equal access for women and men to every role in the church. Others, often called complementarians, hold that the verse speaks of equal standing in salvation while other passages govern roles in church and home. Both groups affirm the verse's plain point: in Christ there is no second-class believer. Christians also later drew on this text in arguing against slavery.

questions: Paul asks the Galatians to remember how they first received the Spirit. What difference does it make to remember how your own faith began?
Why do you think people who start with grace so often drift toward earning their standing with God by performance?
If all believers are one in Christ, what divisions in your church or community most need to be challenged by that truth?
